question: What is the OWASP Top 10 and why should every backend developer know it?
title: OWASP Top 10 Overview – Java Backend Developer Guide
direct_answer: **OWASP Top 10** — A consensus list of the most critical web application security risks, updated periodically. Knowing it gives backend developers a baseline vocabulary and awareness of common attack vectors. It's referenced in security reviews, compliance requirements, and interviews.

interviewer_intent.testing: Security awareness breadth — does this developer think about security proactively?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting the list without explaining what each item means or why it matters
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain 3-4 items in your own words with a concrete Java example for each

sections.title: OWASP Top 10 (2021 Edition)
sections.content:
**A01: Broken Access Control** — Users can access resources or actions they shouldn't. Example: any user can access `/api/admin` because authorization is missing. Fix: @PreAuthorize, proper role checks.

**A02: Cryptographic Failures** — Sensitive data transmitted or stored unprotected. Example: passwords in plaintext, HTTP instead of HTTPS. Fix: bcrypt, HTTPS, encrypted fields.

**A03: Injection** — Attacker-controlled data is interpreted as code. Includes SQL injection, LDAP injection. Fix: parameterized queries, PreparedStatement.

**A04: Insecure Design** — Security not built into design from the start. Fix: threat modeling, security requirements, secure defaults.

**A05: Security Misconfiguration** — Default credentials, unnecessary services, verbose error messages. Fix: harden defaults, disable unused endpoints, proper error handling.

**A06: Vulnerable Components** — Using libraries with known CVEs. Fix: dependency scanning (OWASP Dependency Check), keep dependencies updated.

**A07: Authentication Failures** — Weak passwords, credential stuffing, missing MFA. Fix: strong password policies, bcrypt, rate limiting.

**A08: Data Integrity Failures** — Software updates, CI/CD pipelines without integrity checks. Includes deserialization vulnerabilities.

**A09: Logging Failures** — Insufficient logging means attacks go undetected. Fix: log auth failures, rate limit violations, access to sensitive resources.

**A10: SSRF** — Server-Side Request Forgery — server fetches attacker-controlled URLs.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A01 (Broken Access Control) and A03 (Injection) are the most commonly exploited
- A06 (Vulnerable Components) is highly relevant — most Java projects use dozens of dependencies
- A09 (Logging Failures) is often ignored by freshers — security events must be logged
- OWASP provides free tools: ZAP (web scanner), Dependency Check (CVE scanner)
- The list updates periodically — 2021 is the current version
- Each item has detailed documentation at owasp.org

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The OWASP Top 10 is a list of the most critical web application security risks. The ones most relevant to Java backend developers are: Injection (A03) — SQL injection via unparameterized queries, which PreparedStatement and JPA prevent; Broken Access Control (A01) — missing authorization checks, which Spring Security's @PreAuthorize and role configuration address; Cryptographic Failures (A02) — weak password storage, which BCryptPasswordEncoder fixes; Security Misconfiguration (A05) — default credentials, exposed actuator endpoints, verbose error messages; and Vulnerable Components (A06) — outdated dependencies with known CVEs, which OWASP Dependency Check can scan for. I think of the Top 10 as a security review checklist: before deploying a feature, I should be able to say how I've addressed each relevant item.

followup_questions: Which OWASP Top 10 item is most often caused by developer mistakes versus infrastructure issues?
How would you check your Spring Boot project for vulnerable dependencies?
What is SSRF and how does it work?

question: What is A01 Broken Access Control and how do you prevent it in Spring Boot?
title: Broken Access Control Prevention in Spring Boot – OWASP A01
direct_answer: **Broken Access Control (OWASP A01)** — Users can access resources or perform actions they shouldn't be permitted to. Most common: missing authorization checks, users accessing other users' data by changing IDs, privilege escalation. Fix: enforce authorization at every access point, not just the UI.

interviewer_intent.testing: Authorization implementation knowledge — the most exploited OWASP category
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking URL-level security is sufficient — attackers bypass UI restrictions; every backend endpoint must check authorization
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the IDOR example: /api/orders/123 — does the current user own order 123?

sections.title: Common Broken Access Control Patterns
Key Points
sections.content:
- IDOR: verify the user owns the resource, not just that they're authenticated
- Check authorization at the service layer, not just URL patterns
- @PreAuthorize for method-level access control
- Never trust user-supplied IDs without ownership verification
- Admin endpoints need explicit ADMIN role check — don't rely on them being 'hidden'
- Audit log all access to sensitive resources

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Broken Access Control means users can access resources or actions they shouldn't. The most common example in REST APIs is IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference. If my API has GET /orders/123 and any authenticated user can retrieve any order just by changing the order ID, that's a broken access control vulnerability. The fix is checking ownership: after loading the order, verify the current user's ID matches the order's owner ID, and throw an AccessDeniedException if not. Spring Security's @PreAuthorize can do this with custom SpEL expressions, or I do the check explicitly in the service layer. The mistake is relying only on URL pattern security — that controls whether you can call the endpoint, but not whether you should have access to this specific record.

question: What is Security Misconfiguration (OWASP A05) and what are common Spring Boot examples?
title: Security Misconfiguration in Spring Boot – OWASP A05
direct_answer: **Security Misconfiguration (OWASP A05)** — Insecure default settings, unnecessary features enabled, verbose error messages, default credentials. Spring Boot examples: Spring Actuator endpoints exposed publicly, H2 console in production, default Swagger UI access, detailed stack traces in error responses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Spring Boot-specific security configuration pitfalls
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Spring Boot's out-of-box defaults can expose sensitive endpoints in production
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name specific Spring Boot misconfigurations and their remediations with properties or config code

sections.title: Spring Boot Security Misconfiguration Examples
sections.content:
**1. Spring Actuator endpoints exposed:**
```properties
# DANGEROUS in production:
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*
# SAFE:
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when_authorized
```

**2. H2 Console in production:**
```properties
# Disable for non-dev profiles:
spring.h2.console.enabled=false
```

**3. Stack traces in error responses:**
```properties
# Don't expose internal details:
server.error.include-stacktrace=never
server.error.include-message=never
```

**4. Default Swagger UI:**
Disable in production or protect with authentication.

**5. Default CORS allow-all:**
```java
// DANGEROUS:
config.addAllowedOrigin("*");  // anyone can call your API cross-origin
// SAFE:
config.addAllowedOrigin("https://yourapp.com");
```

**6. Default credentials:**
Spring Security generates a random password for dev — ensure production has proper config.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Actuator endpoints expose shutdown, env, heap dumps — restrict or protect
- Stack traces in API responses reveal internal structure — always disable
- H2 console in production is a remote code execution risk
- Swagger UI should be disabled or authentication-protected in production
- CORS allow-all (*) is a misconfiguration for most APIs
- Principle: secure defaults, then add access where needed

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Security misconfiguration in Spring Boot often comes from out-of-the-box defaults that are fine for development but dangerous in production. The most critical ones: Spring Actuator endpoints — if you expose all of them publicly, attackers can get environment variables, thread dumps, shutdown the app. I always restrict actuator exposure to health and info only, or move them to a separate management port. Stack traces in error responses are another common mistake — they reveal exception class names, line numbers, and package structure that attackers use to craft exploits. I configure server.error.include-stacktrace=never. H2 console in production is particularly dangerous — it's basically a direct database access interface. CORS configured to allow all origins is also a misconfiguration unless you genuinely have a public API.

question: What is OWASP A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components and how do you address it?
title: Vulnerable Components in Java Projects – OWASP A06
direct_answer: **OWASP A06 Vulnerable Components** — Using dependencies with known CVEs creates exploitable vulnerabilities even in well-written code. Fix: regularly check dependencies with OWASP Dependency Check or Snyk, keep dependencies updated, subscribe to security advisories. Log4Shell (Log4j) was an A06 attack.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness that security isn't just code you write — it's also the code you import
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that outdated dependencies are a top attack vector — Log4Shell affected virtually every Java application
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Log4Shell as a real example: Log4j CVE-2021-44228 affected 93% of cloud environments and required emergency patching

sections.title: Dependency Security in Java Projects
sections.content:
**Why this matters:**
A typical Spring Boot project imports hundreds of transitive dependencies. Any of them may have a known CVE.

**Real example: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228):**
- Log4j 2.0-2.14.1 had JNDI lookup vulnerability
- An attacker could trigger remote code execution by logging attacker-controlled input
- Affected virtually every Java application using Log4j
- Required immediate emergency patching in December 2021

**Tools to scan Java dependencies:**
```bash
# OWASP Dependency Check (Maven plugin)
mvn org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check

# Gradle plugin
plugins { id 'org.owasp.dependencycheck' version '8.0.0' }

# GitHub Dependabot (automatic PR for vulnerable deps)
# Snyk (continuous monitoring)
```

**Best practices:**
- Run dependency scan in CI/CD pipeline — fail build on high severity CVEs
- Use Spring Boot managed versions — BOM manages compatible, tested versions
- Subscribe to Spring Security advisories
- Review changelogs before major upgrades

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- OWASP Dependency Check scans for known CVEs in Maven/Gradle dependencies
- Include dependency scanning in CI/CD — don't wait for manual reviews
- Log4Shell is the most famous Java A06 vulnerability — know it
- Spring Boot's version management helps — but doesn't solve all CVEs
- Transitive dependencies are also scanned — not just direct ones
- GitHub Dependabot creates PRs automatically for vulnerable dependencies

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Vulnerable components mean that well-written application code can still be exploited through the libraries you depend on. The most impactful example in Java was Log4Shell in late 2021 — Log4j had a remote code execution vulnerability that affected virtually every Java application. Organizations had to emergency-patch in the middle of the night because the severity was CVSS 10. In practice, I address this by adding OWASP Dependency Check to the Maven build — it scans all dependencies including transitive ones against the National Vulnerability Database and fails the build if high-severity CVEs are found. For continuous monitoring, GitHub Dependabot or Snyk creates automatic pull requests when a new CVE is published for a dependency you're using. The goal is to catch these in CI/CD, not after a breach.

followup_questions: What was Log4Shell and why was it so severe?
How do you integrate OWASP Dependency Check into a Maven build?
What is a CVE and how do you find out if one affects your project?

question: What security headers should a Spring Boot REST API return?
title: Security Headers for Spring Boot REST APIs – OWASP Guide
direct_answer: **Security headers** — Spring Security adds many by default: X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, X-XSS-Protection, HSTS, Referrer-Policy. For APIs: also configure CSP and CORS properly. These headers are a low-cost, high-value defense layer enforced by browsers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of browser-level security controls via HTTP headers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Spring Security already adds several security headers by default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the headers Spring Security adds by default and explain what each does — shows you understand the framework, not just the concept

sections.title: Spring Security Default Headers
sections.content:
**Spring Security adds these by default:**

- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` — Prevents MIME-type sniffing. Browser uses declared Content-Type, not guessing.
- `X-Frame-Options: DENY` — Prevents clickjacking by blocking iframes embedding your pages.
- `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block` — Legacy XSS filter for older browsers (modern browsers use CSP).
- `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` — Forces HTTPS.
- `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate` — Prevents sensitive page caching.
- `Pragma: no-cache` — Legacy cache control.

**You should add:**
```java
http.headers()
  .contentSecurityPolicy("default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'")
  .and()
  .referrerPolicy(ReferrerPolicy.STRICT_ORIGIN_WHEN_CROSS_ORIGIN);
```

**Check with:**
- security headers.com — analyzes headers for your URL
- Mozilla Observatory — comprehensive security scan

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Spring Security adds 6 security headers by default — no config needed for these
- X-Frame-Options prevents clickjacking
- HSTS forces HTTPS for future requests
- X-Content-Type-Options prevents MIME sniffing vulnerabilities
- CSP is NOT added by default — you need to configure it
- Use securityheaders.com to verify your production headers

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Spring Security adds several security headers automatically when you include it as a dependency. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff prevents MIME type sniffing attacks. X-Frame-Options: DENY prevents your pages from being embedded in iframes, which stops clickjacking attacks. HSTS forces all future requests to use HTTPS after the first secure connection. Cache-Control prevents sensitive responses from being cached by intermediaries. These are free security improvements just from having Spring Security in your project. What you need to add explicitly is Content Security Policy — Spring Security provides the configuration method but doesn't set a default policy because it's application-specific. I also recommend checking your production headers against securityheaders.com, which grades your header configuration and highlights missing or misconfigured headers.

followup_questions: What is a clickjacking attack and how does X-Frame-Options prevent it?
How do you verify which security headers your Spring Boot app is returning?
Why doesn't Spring Security set a Content Security Policy by default?
